blocks.text: **"You are seeing a 28-year-old woman for her first antenatal booking visit. Take an appropriate antenatal history."**
"Take a booking history from this pregnant woman."
"A 32-year-old G2P1 presents at 12 weeks for antenatal booking. Take a complete history."

subsections.subsection_title: 2. WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF BOOKING?

items.text: Establish the expected date of delivery
Identify complications in the current pregnancy
Determine whether specialist/high-risk care is required

blocks.text: "Good morning. My name is Dr ___. I'm one of the doctors looking after you."
"Could I confirm your name and age, please?"
"I'd like to take a detailed history about your pregnancy, previous pregnancies and general health. This helps us identify anything that could affect you or your baby and plan your antenatal care."
Don't assume the patient's stated gestational age is correct.
"How did you find out that you were pregnant?"
**"What was the first day of your last menstrual period?"**
"How long is your usual menstrual cycle?"
This is important because dating based on an uncertain LMP can be inaccurate.
Then compare this with any dating ultrasound.
"Have you had an ultrasound scan during this pregnancy?"
If an early ultrasound provides reliable dating, it may be used to establish gestational age according to the applicable dating protocol.
"How many times have you been pregnant, including this pregnancy?"
"How many pregnancies have reached the stage where you delivered?"
A woman with two children may have been pregnant five times.

content_groups.group_title: WHEN → HOW FAR → HOW DELIVERED → BABY → COMPLICATIONS

blocks.text: "How many weeks were you when you delivered?"
"Was the delivery vaginal or by caesarean section?"
"Was there any complication during the pregnancy or delivery?"
If there was a previous CS, ask:
"How many caesarean sections have you had?"
"What was the reason for the caesarean?"
"Did you have any vaginal deliveries before or after the caesarean?"
"Do you have the previous operative records?"
This becomes particularly important when discussing:
"Have you ever had high blood pressure during a previous pregnancy?"
A previous pregnancy complicated by severe pre-eclampsia makes the current pregnancy higher risk.
"Have you ever been diagnosed with diabetes during a previous pregnancy?"
"Have you ever delivered a baby before 37 weeks?"
This can significantly influence management of the current pregnancy.
Now move chronologically through the current pregnancy.
"When did you first feel the baby move?"
"Have the baby's movements been normal recently?"
"When did you last feel the baby move normally?"
This is particularly important in later pregnancy.
"Any blurring of your vision or flashing lights?"
"Any pain in the upper abdomen, particularly under the ribs?"
"Have you noticed sudden swelling of your face or hands?"
"Have you been told your blood pressure is high?"
Then ask whether glucose testing has been performed.
"Have you been told that you are anaemic?"
This is one of the most important components of booking.
"Have you ever had a blood clot in your legs or lungs?"
**"Have you ever had an operation on your uterus?"**
"Do you have any allergies to medicines or anything else?"
"Are you up to date with your vaccinations?"
Depending on the local antenatal programme and patient circumstances, review relevant vaccination status.
Some vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy while others are recommended depending on circumstances.

items.text: Intellectual disability with possible genetic cause

blocks.text: "Is there any family history of inherited disease or babies born with congenital abnormalities?"
"Do you know your blood group and Rhesus status?"
This becomes particularly important in Rh-negative pregnancy.
"Has anyone ever physically hurt or threatened you?"
"Has anyone ever forced you to have sexual contact?"
"Do you ever eat non-food substances such as soil, chalk or ice?"
Pica can be associated with iron deficiency.
**"What investigations would you request at booking?"**
A good answer should be **structured**, not a random list.

items.text: Other infection screening based on risk/local guidelines

blocks.text: Risk-based assessment and/or formal screening according to local protocol.
Screening is different from diagnostic testing.
At the end of the booking history, ask yourself:

content_groups.group_title: Is this pregnancy low risk or high risk?

subsections.subsection_title: 38. HOW TO PRESENT A BOOKING HISTORY

blocks.text: "This is a 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 11 weeks and 4 days' gestation by an early dating ultrasound. Her LMP was reliable and is consistent with the ultrasound dating."
"She booked for antenatal care at 10 weeks and has had no vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or significant vomiting. She reports normal general health."
"Her previous pregnancy was delivered at term by spontaneous vaginal delivery and was complicated by gestational hypertension but no eclampsia or postpartum haemorrhage."
"She has no significant medical or surgical history and takes folic acid and iron supplementation. She has no known drug allergies."
"She does not smoke, drink alcohol or use recreational drugs. There are no significant family or safeguarding concerns identified."

"Her pregnancy would therefore require particular attention to her previous hypertensive disorder, and I would review her blood pressure, baseline investigations and antenatal screening and formulate an appropriate surveillance plan."

"This is a 35-year-old G3P1+1 at 10 weeks' gestation with one previous term delivery and one previous miscarriage. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by severe pre-eclampsia requiring delivery at 32 weeks."
"She also has chronic hypertension and is currently taking antihypertensive medication."
"She has no current symptoms suggestive of pre-eclampsia."
This is **not simply a routine booking**.

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What is the most important thing to establish at booking?

blocks.text: **Gestational age and expected date of delivery, while simultaneously identifying maternal, obstetric and fetal risk factors.**
Add seven days to the first day of the LMP, subtract three months and add one year, assuming a regular 28-day cycle.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What factors make a pregnancy high risk?

blocks.text: Significant maternal disease, previous adverse obstetric outcomes, current pregnancy complications, multiple pregnancy, fetal abnormalities and important social or safeguarding concerns.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What would you ask about a previous caesarean section?

blocks.text: Number of CS, indication, timing, operative complications, type of uterine incision if known, subsequent vaginal deliveries, recovery and availability of operative records.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. Why ask about previous pre-eclampsia?

blocks.text: Because it increases the risk of hypertensive disease in a subsequent pregnancy and influences antenatal risk assessment and preventive management.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. Why ask about previous stillbirth?

blocks.text: It may identify potentially recurrent maternal, placental, fetal or genetic factors and indicates the need for careful review and appropriate surveillance in the current pregnancy.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ Mistake 1: Treating booking as just an LMP history

blocks.text: **Cardiac → renal → endocrine → neurological → haematological → autoimmune → infectious.**
Some medications can significantly affect pregnancy.
Pregnancy can be an important opportunity to identify domestic abuse.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ Mistake 6: Giving every pregnant woman the same investigation plan

blocks.title: Investigations and screening should be tailored to:

blocks.text: "This is a __-year-old G_P woman at ___ weeks' gestation, dated by ___, with an EDD of ___. She booked at ___ weeks. The current pregnancy has been complicated by ___ / has been uncomplicated so far. Her previous obstetric history is significant for ___. She has/does not have significant medical or surgical conditions. She is taking ___ and has ___ allergies. Her relevant family and social history includes ___. The important risk factors I have identified are ___. I would now complete her examination, review her antenatal investigations and arrange any additional investigations or specialist input required according to her risk profile."
